title: Maximum-likelihood noise degrades sample quality
description: The authors note that density-based maximum-likelihood models require adding noise to cover low-dimensional supports, and this added noise degrades the quality of samples and makes images blurry.

verdict.reasoning: The single deep-read paper directly engages the gap: it proposes Tweedie-based and conditional denoising mechanisms intended to let likelihood-based models trained with added Gaussian noise sample as though no noise had been added. It evaluates VAEs and normalizing flows on several image benchmarks. However, the paper's own empirical results show that the denoising methods only sporadically improve over simply adding noise or not adding it, with only a couple of non-marginal gains and some variants even hurting performance. It does not establish a general mechanism that reliably recovers unblurred, high-quality samples, and it does not directly demonstrate reduction of noise-induced blur. Thus a meaningful part of the problem has been explored but the core remains open, so the gap is only partially addressed.

paper.title: Denoising Deep Generative Models
paper.abstract: Likelihood-based deep generative models have recently been shown to exhibit pathological behaviour under the manifold hypothesis as a consequence of using high-dimensional densities to model data with low-dimensional structure. In this paper we propose two methodologies aimed at addressing this problem. Both are based on adding Gaussian noise to the data to remove the dimensionality mismatch during training, and both provide a denoising mechanism whose goal is to sample from the model as though no noise had been added to the data. Our first approach is based on Tweedie's formula, and the second on models which take the variance of added noise as a conditional input. We show that surprisingly, while well motivated, these approaches only sporadically improve performance over not adding noise, and that other methods of addressing the dimensionality mismatch are more empirically adequate.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly targets the gap's problem: it addresses the dimensionality mismatch that forces likelihood-based models to add Gaussian noise, and proposes two denoising mechanisms (Tweedie-based denoising and conditional denoising where σ is a conditioning input) whose explicit goal is "to sample from the model as though no noise had been added to the data," i.e., to counteract the noise-induced sample-quality degradation. It evaluates these on VAEs and normalizing flows across MNIST, FMNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10 using FID. The empirical finding, however, is that both methods only sporadically improve over simply adding noise (or not adding it), so the proposed fix works only in limited cases.
assessments.what_remains_open: The core of the gap remains open: the paper's own results show that its denoising procedures "do not provide meaningful empirical improvements" and "only sporadically improve performance over not adding noise," with the only non-marginal gains being CD-VAE on SVHN and CD-NF on MNIST, and some denoising variants even harming performance. Consequently, no general mechanism is established that lets maximum-likelihood density models trained with added noise reliably produce unblurred, high-quality samples; the paper explicitly concludes that better methods for handling the noise/dimensionality mismatch are needed and leaves the problem for future work. (Note also that the paper frames the issue through manifold overfitting and FID rather than through explicit blurriness artifacts, so a direct demonstration of reducing noise-induced blur is not provided.)

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: This is a tractable, methodologically mature problem. Data are standard image benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA) requiring no new collection or labeling, and VAE/flow experiments run on modest GPU hardware. The approach space is rich with known tools—Tweedie's formula, conditional denoising, learned post-hoc denoisers, score-based purification—so progress can come from extending existing methods rather than a fundamental breakthrough. Success is measurable via established metrics (FID, sample sharpness/blur, log-likelihood), and the problem can be scoped to a specific model family and benchmark. The main feasibility risk is methodological: the prior attempt showed only sporadic gains, so a reliable, general mechanism is not trivial to find, which keeps this below 1.0.
